DILG OPINION No. 23 s. 2024 FEB O.: HON. JEANNIE SANDOVAL Mayor, Malabon City Dear Mayor Sandoval: We write your good Office regarding the letter dated August 29, 2023 from Atty. Juan Miguel E. Montoro, Manila Teacher's Mutual Aid System, Inc. (MTMASI) concerning the application for business permit renewal of MTMASI. As represented in the subject letter, hereunder are the pertinent factual antecedents: • On June 14, 2023, Business Permit Licensing Officer (BPLO), Mr. Russel G. Besabe, verbally denied the application for renewal of MTMASI solely for the reason that since the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas revoked the license to operate of Manila Teachers Savings and Loan Association Inc. (MTSLAI), it therefore follows that MTMASl's should also cease its operations, alleging that the two (2) corporations are one and the same. • On July 17, 2023, a meeting was held with the key officials of Malabon in order to discuss the difference between MTMASI and MTSLAI and why regulations and resolutions issued by one company do not apply to another. • Thereafter, MTMASI sent a letter conveying that MTMASI is a distinct business entity from MTSLAI, and that, any regulation, decision, or resolution issued or made applicable to MTSLAI should not be made automatically applicable to MTMASI. • However, the key officials of Malabon City remained steadfast in arguing and maintaining that the MTSLAI and MTMASI are the same entities, and any regulation issued and directed against the MTSLAI should also be made applicable to the MTMASI. Premised from the foregoing, MTMASI belabors that the denial of the request for a business permit by the key officials of Malabon City was done in violation of Section 7 of Republic Act 11032, or the Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018, as there was no formal written explanation, notice, or document detailing the reason for the denial of MTMASI's application. At the outset, Section 455(b)(3)(iv) of the Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act 7160, hereinafter referred to as the Code) provides that: "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline NO.: 8876-34-54

"Section 455. Chief Executive; Powers, Duties and Compensation. (a) Xxx (b) For efficient, effective and economical governance the purpose of which is the general welfare of the city and its inhabitants pursuant to Section 16 of this Code, the city mayor shall: xxx xxx XXX (3) Initiate and maximize the generation of resources and revenues, and apply the same to the implementation of development plans, program objectives and priorities as provided for under Section 18 of this Code, particularly those resources and revenues programmed for agro-industrial development and countryside growth and progress and, relative thereto, shall: xxx xxx xxx (iv) Issue licenses and permits and suspend or revoke the same for any violation of the conditions upon which said licenses or permits had been issued, pursuant to law or ordinance. xxx xxx xxx The Supreme Court has elucidated that "permits and licenses are issued for regulatory purposes and under certain condition upon which they are issued pursuant to a law or ordinance, the entitlement thereof is not a matter of right but a privilege, and neither is it a property. A license or a permit is not a contract between the sovereignty and the licensee or permitee, and is not a property in the constitutional sense, as to which the constitutional proscription against impairment of the obligation of contracts may extend. A license is rather in the nature of a special privilege, of a permission or authority to do what is within its terms. It is not in any way vested, permanent or absolute. 1 Parenthetically, the Supreme Court, in Alfredo Lim and Rafaelido v. The Court of Appeals et al. ruled that: "[The] power of the mayor to issue business licenses and permits necessarily includes the corollary power to suspend, revoke or even refuse to issue the same. However, the power to suspend or revoke these licenses and permits is expressly premised on the violation of the conditions of these permits and licenses. The laws specifically refer to the violation of the condition(s) on which the licenses and permits were issued. Similarly, the power to refuse to issue licenses and permits is premised on non-compliance with the prerequisites for the issuance of such licenses and permits. The mayor must observe due process in exercising these powers, which means that the mayor must give the applicant or licensee notice and opportunity to be heard. " This Department, in view of its supervisory function over local government, reiterates herein attached DILG-ARTA Joint Memorandum Circular No. 2021-012, dated November 19, 2021 , specifically Item 6 (sub-item: Business Processing and Licensing Office (BPLO)), which provides that: 1 Acebed0 optical Company, Inc. vs. CA, GR. No. 100152, dated March 31, 2000: DILG Legal Opinion No. 33, s. 2011 2Entitled, GUIDELINES ON STREAMLINING OF LGU SYSTEMS AND PROCEDURES AON BUSINESS AND NONBUSINESS-RELATED SERVICES FOR CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES Page 2 Of 4

Applications for Business Permits and related clearances or licenses, both for new and renewal, shall be governed by the provisions of ARTA-DTI-DILG-DICT JMC No. I, Series of 2021, dated 13 April 2021, or the "Guidelines for Processing Business Permits, Related Clearances and Licenses in All Cities and Municipalities. "Hence, all requirements, steps processing times, and cost for these transactions shall comply with said JMC and its Operation Manual Implementing the same. Corollary thereto, Item 8.2.1 (sub-Item: Business Permit Renewal Applications) states: 8.2 Standard Documentary Requirements 8.2. I LGUs shall limit the documentary requirements for business permit applications to be submitted together with the UAF to those listed below: xxx xxx xxx Business Permit Renewal Applications a) Proof Of annual gross receipts which may include: i) Audited financial statements ('AFS") or unaudited AFS for those who are not required to file AFS with the BIR or ii) Sworn declaration of gross sales or receipts; or iii) Income tax returns Having laid down the foregoing, attention is now respectfully directed to the pronouncement of the Supreme Court in Lacap v. Sandiganbayan and the People of the Philippines (G.R. No. 198162, dated June 21, 2017), which is fundamental to the resolution of the herein issue. The Supreme Court ruled that: "In an application for a mayor's permit or license to do business in a municipality or city, the procedure is fairly standard and uncomplicated. It requires the submission of the required documents and the payment of the assessed business taxes and fees. In case of failure to comply with the requirements, the application deserves to be disapproved. If the application is compliant, then approval is the action to be taken. An inaction or refusal to act is a course of action anathema to public service with utmost responsibility and efficiency. If the deliberate refusal to act or intentional inaction on an application for mayor's permit is motivated by personal conflicts and political considerations, it thus becomes discriminatory, and constitutes a violation Of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act." This Department has consistently opined that the issuance of business permit is an administrative function of the mayor; the issuance thereof depends on whether or not all the requirements set forth by law or ordinance for its issuance are met/submitted. Stated differently, in case an applicant has complied with all the requirements, it behooves the mayor to act or approve such an application—the application cannot be arbitrarily denied. Along this line, it should be emphasized that deliberate refusal to issue business permits denotes a flagrant and culpable unwillingness to perform a duty as mandated by law. Those responsible for such delay or refusal will be opening themselves to a possible administrative case of dereliction of duty, neglect of duty, or abuse of authority as may be warranted by evidence, which are grounds for disciplinary action pursuant to the Code. Pertinently, the Supreme Court beseeches in Nessia v. Fermin (G.R. No. 102918, March 30, 1993), "Public officials are called upon to act expeditiously on matters pending before them. For only in acting thereon either by signifying approval or disapproval may the plaintiff continue on to the next step of the bureaucratic process. On the other hand, official inaction brings to a standstill the administrative process and the plaintiff is left in the darkness of uncertainty." Page 3 of 4

Per our evaluation of the facts as represented by MTMASI, the inaction or refusal of Malabon City vis-å-vis the renewal of the business permit applicant of MTMASI solely for the alleged indistinct entity of MTMASI from the MTSLAI appears to be unreasonable. As has been established, the MTMASI is separate and distinct from the MTSLAI based on the attached certification issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Hence, our referral of the herein letter of MTMASI to your good Office hoping that you could re-evaluate the issue raised taking into account our discussion above. Nevertheless, if there be other issues which were not represented by MTMASI, we will be glad to hear from you the soonest. Thank you. Very truly yours, By the Authority of the Secreta OR R.
